claims.text: A nanometer-scale adaptive interfacial coating can trigger in situ formation of an oxide tribofilm on CoCrFeNi during sliding.
The generated oxide tribofilm will be dynamic and self-replenishing.
The generated oxide tribofilm will be lubricious.
The coating and tribofilm will minimize friction and wear from room temperature to 800 °C.
The proposed intervention is deposition of a nanometer-scale adaptive interfacial coating engineered to catalyze lubricious-oxide formation during sliding.
The oxide tribofilm forms at the coating interface and adapts dynamically to temperature changes.
The coating promotes controlled surface oxidation during sliding through temperature-driven catalytic reactions.
The adaptive oxide layer reduces metal-to-metal contact.
Reducing metal-to-metal contact lowers friction and wear at both low and high temperatures.
Relative to uncoated CoCrFeNi, the coated sample will have a lower and more consistent coefficient of friction throughout the room-temperature-to-800 °C range.
Relative to uncoated CoCrFeNi, the coated sample will have a lower wear rate throughout the room-temperature-to-800 °C range.
The intervention requires sufficient oxygen to sustain induced oxidation.
Highly corrosive agents are outside the expected effective operating environment.
Loads exceeding the coating's mechanical limits are outside the expected effective operating range.
The magnitude of friction and wear improvement likely depends on coating composition, coating thickness, and reaction kinetics at different temperatures.
